extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism students, policy analysts, and journalists interested in news selection and media democracy
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the desirability, feasibility, and likely effects of multiperspectival (multi‑perspective) news and the organizational, political, and economic criteria that bear on selecting and producing national news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiperspectival news furthers democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental justification for multiperspectival news is its potential for furthering democracy. Multiperspectival news is not designed to gain supporters for any specific political cause; rather, it will enable people to obtain news relevant to their own perspectives, and therefore to their own interests and political goals. In the process, the symbolic arena would become more democratic, for the symbolic power of now dominant sources and perspectives would be reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a normative criterion: evaluate proposals by how much they enable diverse audiences to obtain news relevant to their perspectives and by how much they reduce the symbolic dominance of current sources. Note limits discussed: multiperspectival news is political and redistributive (it changes symbolic power), and its democratic effect is partial and contingent on broader social/economic structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of funding (non-commercial, non-governmental ideal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideally, news organizations should be non-commercial and nongovernmental bodies, obtaining funds from various sources without any strings attached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat funding independence as a quality standard but note the caution: the experience of public television suggests this ideal is illusory. Assess realistic funding models and the extent to which they introduce constraints or strings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of government-run media for diversity (with caveats)
rubrics_metrics.description: Government news media would add to the diversity of national news. Government news media would relieve the commercial news media of the need and incentive to publicize official sources, thus releasing additional air time or print space for other sources and strengthening the adversarial posture of commercial journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating government media, weigh gains in diversity and indirect benefits to commercial outlets against predictable objections from commercial competitors and risks of government influence or pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda-setting capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: The news media redistribute symbolic power when they act as agenda setters, helping place and publicize issues in the symbolic arena, and thereby increasing the influence of supporters of these issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess news initiatives by their likely agenda-setting effects: what new issues will be placed on the public agenda, which constituencies will gain influence, and whether multiperspectival approaches broaden the range of agendas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of moral disorder reporting to influence opinion (contingent and partly fortuitous)
rubrics_metrics.description: The news disseminates facts, particularly about moral disorder. In the right place and at the right time, moral disorder news can create a wave of sympathy or antipathy, tipping public opinion, and power, on those issues in which public opinion counts. The conditions under which this happens, however, are partly fortuitous; and journalists cannot, by themselves, automatically tip public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume predictable causal power of reporting. Evaluate the plausibility that particular moral disorder stories will resonate and tip opinion, and acknowledge the role of timing, context, and luck.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic appraisal of news' limits to redistribute power
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiperspectival news will not, therefore, bring about further democratization of America by itself. Democracy is a property of social structure, not symbols, requiring greater equalization of power and of people's ability to exert pressure on their government. Power cannot be equalized without economic change, for unequal economic power breeds unequal political power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure proposed news reforms against realistic expectations: news can supply necessary information but is insufficient to alter economic and political hierarchies on its own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation of institutional and political opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiperspectival news is likely to encounter opposition, and not only from public officials and others objecting to sharing the news with additional sources. Example: Finnish television's multiperspectival policy (1965–1970) was opposed by conservative newspapers and many established institutions and was abolished after a conservative government was elected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate feasibility by mapping likely opponents (commercial media, established institutions, conservative political actors) and by considering mechanisms through which they might resist or roll back reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulnerability of government-run or single-medium reforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Finnish television, being government-run, was vulnerable to begin with; even so, a single American news medium instituting a similar policy might be vulnerable as well, both to commercial and government pressure, and to opposition from other news media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the institutional durability of reforms: government-run solutions may be especially exposed to political change; single-outlet reforms can be undermined by external pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and heterogeneity affect feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: America is larger and more heterogeneous than Finland; equivalent 'established institutions' could coalesce sufficiently amongst themselves or with a conservative federal government, making multiperspectival policies harder to sustain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for national scale, heterogeneity, and institutional density when extrapolating from smaller-country examples; feasibility in one polity may not transfer to another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normative trade-off: cohesion versus representation of diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the news media should aim to depict America as a cohesive unit or as an array of diverse, often conflicting groups depends on one's political values. For those who believe that cohesion and order are prime national and societal goals, multiperspectivism would be objectionable. For those who feel that the interests of diverse groups have priority over the needs of nation and society, multiperspectival news and some decentralization of the national media are preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit the normative choices embedded in news-selection policies and evaluate them according to the values (cohesion vs representation) prioritized by stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential for increased factual/interest-based cohesion
rubrics_metrics.description: If more people obtain news relevant to their interests, and if that news helps them achieve their own goals, they may feel themselves to be part of a larger whole. In the long run, then, the country would be more cohesive in fact if not in symbol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider downstream effects on civic belonging: representation of interests can build factual cohesion even if symbolic unity declines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for public demand to make multiperspectival news effective
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiperspectival news does supply some of the necessary information. However, it would be a good deal more effective if it coincided with widespread public demand for greater popular representation in the economy and the polity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate market and civic demand: reforms are more likely to succeed and matter if there is broad public appetite for the kinds of representation offered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentive structures of journalists and firms
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists have little incentive for significant change. They, or at least their firms, would have even less incentive for multiperspectivism because it undercuts the twin bases of the present journalistic enterprise: efficiency and the power of sources. Journalists might be prepared to reduce the power of present sources, but I doubt that they would accept proposals that created new pressures on them and their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether proposed changes align with or conflict with existing incentives (efficiency, relationships with sources). Reforms that impose extra burdens or reduce predictability are likely to face internal resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic and demographic conditions can drive demand for different news
rubrics_metrics.description: If the current decline in economic growth becomes permanent... people will become more aware... of their own economic and political interests. But insofar as these interests will, in a stratified society like America, be diverse, they will need something very much like multiperspectival news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider macroeconomic and social trends when forecasting demand for multiperspectival formats; shifts in material interests can change audience priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profit motive and willingness-to-pay determine firm response
rubrics_metrics.description: The news firms... exist to make a profit; and if people require a different kind of news and are willing to pay for it, directly or through advertisers, the firms can be expected to go along.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate business models: direct payment, advertiser support, or other revenue mechanisms that would enable firms to adopt multiperspectival strategies without sacrificing profitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of firms' dependence on current holders of power
rubrics_metrics.description: The news firms, more so than the journalists, are sufficiently beholden to various current holders of economic and political power to be reluctant to respond to popular demands for changes in the government and the economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze ownership structures, advertising dependencies, and elite ties that constrain editorial autonomy and make responsiveness to popular demands less likely.
